slides.title: You Bought a Bond. Who Pays You, and When?
lines: Government and corporate IOUs, coupons, market price and what can go wrong.
A BOND IS A PROMISE. NOT A BANK ACCOUNT.
Your contractual cash flows are different from the price another investor offers today.

slides.title: If the bond pays 4%, why can its price fall?
lines: “I receive the same coupon. Why does my investment show a loss?”
Because the market reprices the value of all remaining payments.

slides.title: Follow the money — and the creditor’s claim
lines: A bondholder owns a debt claim, not a slice of a company’s future stock upside.

slides.title: The coupon is set against face value
lines: Illustrative annual equivalent; US Treasury notes/bonds actually pay semiannually.
A 4% coupon is not a promise that your total return is 4%.

slides.title: One bond has several different yield concepts
lines: The purchase price matters as much as the printed coupon.

slides.title: Why a price discount develops
lines: Bond price must drop to offer a higher yield on unchanged contractual cash flows.
Selling before maturity may crystallise a mark-to-market loss.

slides.title: What is the borrower able to promise?
lines: Sovereign repayment capacity, currency/inflation risk, interest-rate risk and settlement conventions.
Contractual claims against a business; earnings, leverage, refinancing and default/recovery risk.
A strong company is not automatically a risk-free creditor investment.

slides.title: Creditors do not all stand in the same queue
lines: Claim may be backed by named collateral; priority depends on legal terms.
General company claim above subordinated obligations.
Lower recovery priority, often demands extra return.
Always read actual indentures and insolvency jurisdiction before ranking claims.

slides.title: Why a company pays more than a Treasury
lines: Hypothetical same-maturity benchmark; real spread includes credit, liquidity and option effects.
A 250bp premium is compensation for risks, not extra free income.

slides.title: Treasuries can rally while a company bond falls
lines: Δ CORP ≈ Δ TREASURY + Δ SPREAD
Illustrative matched tenor and spread definition.
Yield rises 70bp, pressuring the corporate bond price.

slides.title: The clauses that beginners often miss
lines: The issuer may redeem early; attractive coupons may not last.
May be exchangeable for equity; optionality alters value.
Contract restrictions and triggers can protect or limit holders.
The ETF generally does not mature like a bond you hold to maturity.
Yield-to-call and duration can matter more than headline coupon.

slides.title: What happens if you hold rather than sell?
lines: If the issuer pays in full, scheduled principal and coupons arrive; reinvestment and inflation remain.
You receive market price, which may reflect higher rates, wider spreads, low liquidity or credit deterioration.
Even holding to maturity does not eliminate credit, inflation or opportunity cost.

slides.title: Before buying a corporate IOU
lines: Can operations support interest and principal?
When must debt refinance, and at what rate?
Where are you in the legal claim waterfall?
Does yield compensate for default, downgrade and liquidity risk?

lines: Do bond ETF shares promise par at a set maturity?
